title: Numerical derivatives
summary: Approximate a derivative from function values, and see why the centred version is so much better.
intro: The **derivative** f′(x) is the slope of f at x: how fast the output changes per unit change of input. Gradient descent uses derivatives to decide which way to move every weight.

You can approximate it from two function values. The forward difference (f(x + h) − f(x)) / h has error proportional to h. The **central difference** (f(x + h) − f(x − h)) / 2h cancels the first error term, so its error shrinks like h².

Too small an h loses accuracy to rounding, so values around 1e-4 to 1e-6 work well in double precision. Comparing an analytic gradient with a central difference, a **gradient check**, is the standard way to catch backprop bugs.
formula: f′(x) ≈ (f(x + h) − f(x − h)) / (2h)     error ∝ h²
prompt: Write `central_difference(coeffs, x, h)` that returns the central-difference estimate of the derivative of the polynomial with coefficients `coeffs` (highest power first, as used by `np.polyval`) at x.
starter:
import numpy as np

def central_difference(coeffs, x, h):
    f = lambda t: np.polyval(coeffs, t)
    # A forward difference is less accurate; centre it.
    return (f(x + h) - f(x)) / h
hints: Evaluate at x + h and x − h.
explanation: For x³ at 2 the true slope is 3 × 2² = 12. The central difference with h = 0.001 is 12.000001: an error of h². The forward difference gives about 12.006, an error of order h. For any quadratic the central difference is exact, apart from rounding.
